extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners of humor, theatre, literary aesthetics, and comedy-writing
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic theory describing the forms and mechanisms that produce the comic in literature and on stage, with examples and guidance for playwrights and critics about how comic effects are generated and sustained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical repetition / automatism (Jack-in-the-box)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic effect arises when an individual's avarice/impulse is 'automatically' repressed and then springs up again; a mechanical repetition of a sentence or exclamation expresses a fixed idea and indicates automatism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Harpagon's repeated 'No dowry wanted!' or the repeated regret about money. The repetition becomes laughable because it reveals a fixed idea acting like a repeating-machine inside a living person. Use repeated verbal or behavioral ticks to show the mechanisation of character; escalation of tone can intensify the laugh. Caution: repetition should point to an inner automatism, not merely be gratuitous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double personality / inner duel
rubrics_metrics.description: A scene can be comic when it is really between a character and himself — two opposing internal forces (e.g., frankness vs politeness) produce oscillation and repeated attempts at repression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Alceste's 'I don't say that!' repeated as an effort to repress an impulse; the comic arises from seeing one man become two, each preventing the other. The writer should create distinct opposing impulses within one character so that the oscillation becomes mechanical and observable; the intensifying internal tension 'goes off with a bang.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Dancing-jack / manipulation by another (marionette image)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters who seem to act freely but are, from a standpoint, mere toys manipulated by another — the impression of being pulled by strings produces comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Scapin manipulating Geronte and Argante; characters who vacillate between contrary opinions with personified opposing decisions. Authors should personify the opposing decisions or provide characters who play the role of 'string-holders' so the spectator perceives the mechanical arrangement. Spectators instinctively side with the knaves who control the marionettes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Snow-ball / cumulative escalation (arithmetical progression)
rubrics_metrics.description: A small or insignificant cause triggers a succession of events that grow by progression until a large, unexpected effect results — the 'rolling snow-ball' mechanism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: domino-like incidents (caller knocks lady, spills tea, a constable is hit), lawsuits within lawsuits, or a lost letter whose pursuit produces increasingly serious incidents. Use chain reactions where each action triggers the next, increasing momentum and comic stakes. Reversibility/circularity (returning to start) often heightens the effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circularity / return-to-origin (reversibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: A mechanical combination that is reversible or circular — efforts, twists, and turns ultimately bring the situation back to its starting point, producing a comic sense of wasted exertion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the Italian straw hat that keeps eluding capture and then is found eaten; marriages and divorces leading back to the original spouse. Philosophical formulations (Spencer/Kant) describe laughter as reaction to effort ending in void, but the text warns lack of proportion alone isn't sufficient; the comic comes when circularity reveals mechanisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition of situation (dramatic repetition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A situation or combination of circumstances recurs several times in its original form within the moving series of life, contrasting with life's expected irreversibility and producing comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conditions that make this laughable: the repeated scene should be complex yet naturally introduced — the playwright must reconcile those two conditions. Examples: Moliere's plays that reproduce the same incident in multiple 'tempi' (e.g., L'Ecole des femmes or George Dandin). Contemporary authors may instead prepare the audience mentally for coincidences; classical comedy derives repetition from character constancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inversion / topsyturvydom
rubrics_metrics.description: Reversing roles or situations produces comedy — when the expected order is inverted, or an author/plotter is caught in his own trap (robber robbed), the scene becomes comic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the villain who becomes victim of his own villainy; Lawyer Pathelin's client outwitting him; a wife insisting on a rota then falling into a hazard she won't help with. Inversion often becomes a classical type that lends comic resonance to related scenes; even a mere allusion can recall the comic model and make a new scene amusing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal interference of series / equivocal situations
rubrics_metrics.description: A situation is comic when it simultaneously belongs to two independent series of events and can legitimately be interpreted in two entirely different ways (the equivocal situation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stage-made misunderstandings are a special, artificial case: the audience sees both series while characters see only one, producing mistakes and comic oscillation. Authors must repeatedly remind the audience of both the independence and the coincidence of the series (threats of dissolution and recovery) to sustain laughter. The interference may be between concurrent series, or between past and present series (mock-heroic transpositions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanisation of life as the essence of the comic
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic is the perception of a rigid mechanism or automatisms in living continuity — human behavior showing inelasticity, automatism, or movement 'without life' is laughable because it reveals absent-mindedness in life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laughter functions as a social corrective that singles out and represses this form of absent-mindedness. Authors should present behavior that makes characters resemble things (machines) to trigger this corrective laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrast with life: three opposites shaping comic methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Life's outward characteristics are (1) continuous, irreversible evolution in time, (2) complexity and interdependent coexisting elements in space, and (3) perfect individuality; the opposites — repetition, inversion, and reciprocal interference — form the complete abstract formula for methods of comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To design comic situations systematically, take these three counter-characteristics as the archetypes: repetition counters temporal irreversibility, inversion counters expected role order, and reciprocal interference counters individuality/independence of series. These are exhaustive methods of light comedy according to the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation and acceptance of coincidence (contemporary technique)
rubrics_metrics.description: Contemporary light comedy often makes extraordinary coincidences acceptable by preparing or 'mesmerising' the spectator's mind; acceptance by the audience can replace the stage-justification provided by character constancy in classical comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with Moliere: classical repetition is justified by characters' constant forces and moods, whereas modern authors prepare the audience to accept coincidences. Playwrights may choose either technique, but must ensure the audience's suspension of disbelief is cultivated if relying on preparation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personification of opposing decisions (dramatic device)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a character vacillates between two contrary opinions, a comic author personifies the two opposing decisions (or uses separate actors) to hold the 'strings' and make the mechanical oscillation visible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If there's no spectator within the play-world, actors must embody the opposing forces so the audience perceives the mechanical arrangement. This device supports both dancing-jack and inner-duel effects and helps render the oscillation obviously mechanical.
